questions.topic: Intersections of a line and a conic
questions.learningObjective: explain why a line and a conic share at most two points
questions.stem: Explain why a straight line and a non-degenerate conic can have at most two points in common.

answer.exemplar: Write the line as y = mx + b and substitute that single expression for y in the conic. Every conic equation is quadratic in x and y, and after the substitution it is still a polynomial in x alone of degree at most 2, because the highest power of y that appears is y squared and that becomes (mx + b) squared, a quadratic in x. A real polynomial of degree 2 has at most two roots, and each root of that quadratic gives exactly one intersection point, since y is fixed by the line equation once x is known. So the number of common points is at most two. The bound is attained in the ordinary case, and the only ways to see fewer are a tangent, which gives one repeated root, or no real roots at all, which means the line misses the curve. The same reasoning handles a vertical line by solving the conic for x in terms of y instead.

questions.explanation: A model answer must show the substitution turning the conic into a quadratic in one variable, because that is the step that produces the bound of two, and it should say why the degree cannot grow.
questions.hint: Substitute an equation of the line for one of the two variables and count the degree.

questions.learningObjective: explain how the cross-term coefficient determines a rotation angle
questions.stem: Explain how the angle through which the axes must be turned to remove the cross term from a conic's general equation is recovered from the coefficients.

answer.exemplar: Take the general conic Ax squared plus Bxy plus Cy squared plus Dx plus Ey plus F equals 0 and substitute the rotation x = x' cos theta minus y' sin theta, y = x' sin theta plus y' cos theta. Collecting the x'y' terms gives the new mixed coefficient B cos 2 theta plus (C - A) sin 2 theta, and the term is gone exactly when that expression is zero. Dividing through by cos 2 theta turns this into the tangent of 2 theta equal to B over (A - C), which is the recovery rule, and it can be applied without any trigonometry beyond the double-angle identities. Two special cases matter. If A equals C then the denominator vanishes and the mixed coefficient reduces to B cos 2 theta, which is zero for theta of 45 degrees whenever B is zero, that is a circle, and otherwise for the angles that put the new axes on the section's own symmetry lines. And if A minus C is negative the tangent is negative, so the rotation needed is a turn the other way, which is why working out the sign of A - C before rotating saves a wrong turn. The two solutions for 2 theta differ by 180 degrees, so theta and theta plus 90 degrees both remove the term and simply exchange which semi-axis comes first, and the two surviving diagonal coefficients are the eigenvalues of the symmetric matrix with A and C on the diagonal and B over 2 in each off-diagonal slot.

questions.explanation: A model answer must show where the rotated mixed coefficient comes from, since that expression is what produces the recovery rule, and it must deal with the case A equals C where the rule divides by zero.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: explain how one polar formula covers all three conics
questions.stem: Explain how the polar form of a conic shows that a single formula describes an ellipse, a parabola, and a hyperbola at once.

answer.exemplar: Start from the focus-directrix definition with the focus at the pole and the directrix a distance p away along the polar axis. The distance from a point to that directrix measures out as p plus r cos theta, so the definition r equals e times that distance becomes r = e p plus e r cos theta, and rearranging gives r = e p over the quantity 1 plus e cos theta. Only the single number e separates the three conics, and the denominator does all the work. When e is below 1 the quantity 1 plus e cos theta stays between 1 - e and 1 + e, both positive, so r stays finite in every direction and the curve closes on itself, an ellipse. When e is exactly 1 the denominator reaches 0 at the single angle where cos theta equals -1, so r grows without bound in exactly one direction, which is a parabola. When e is above 1 the denominator passes through 0 as the angle sweeps around, so r changes sign there and the single formula traces two separate loops on opposite sides of the pole, a hyperbola. The numerator e p is the semi-latus rectum throughout, the half-length of the focal chord perpendicular to the axis, so that quantity survives the change of shape unchanged.

questions.explanation: A model answer must trace the derivation from the focus-directrix definition and then show how the sign and size of the denominator produce the three different shapes, since that is the unifying idea.
questions.hint: Start from the definition, isolate r, and then ask what the denominator can do for e below, equal to, and above 1.

questions.learningObjective: find the focal distance of a hyperbola with no denominators
questions.stem: The hyperbola with equation 25y squared minus 9x squared equals 225 has its transverse axis along the y-axis. How far is each focus from the centre? Give the answer to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: Dividing by 225 puts the equation in standard form, y squared over 9 minus x squared over 25 equals 1, so a squared = 9 and b squared = 25, and for a hyperbola the two add to give c squared = 34. That makes c the square root of 34, about 5.83. The orientation matters for reading the equation and not for the arithmetic, since the y term being positive is what tells you the curve opens up and down, and the asymptote slope a over b is 3/5 to match.
questions.hint: Divide through by 225, identify which squared length is a and which is b, then add them.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: find a missing semi-axis of an ellipse from the other two measurements
questions.stem: An ellipse has a semi-major axis of length 10, and one of its foci lies 6 units from the centre. What is the length of its semi-minor axis?
questions.explanation: For an ellipse the focal distance c, the semi-major axis a, and the semi-minor axis b satisfy a squared = b squared + c squared. With a = 10 and c = 6, the relation gives 100 = b squared + 36, so b squared is 64 and b = 8. The eccentricity route reaches the same place: e = c/a = 0.6, and b = a times the square root of 1 - e squared, which is 10 times 0.8.
questions.hint: Use the relation that ties the two semi-axes and the focal distance together.

questions.stem: In polar form a conic with its focus at the pole is written as r equals 12 divided by 1 plus 3 sin theta. How far is the directrix from that focus?
questions.explanation: The polar form is r = e p over 1 plus e sin theta, so the numerator 12 is the product e p while the coefficient 3 is the eccentricity, giving p = 12/3 = 4. The directrix is checked by using the definition directly: at theta = 0 the curve is at r = 12, and the directrix is the horizontal line y = 4, so the ratio of the focus distance 12 to the directrix distance 4 is exactly 3, the eccentricity.

questions.learningObjective: measure a chord cut from an ellipse by a line through its centre
questions.stem: The line with equation y equals x cuts the ellipse with equation x squared over 25 plus y squared over 9 equals 1. What is the length of the chord between the two intersection points? Give the answer to two decimal places.
questions.explanation: Putting y = x into the ellipse gives x squared over 25 plus x squared over 9 equals 1, so x squared is 1 divided by the sum of 1/25 and 1/9, which is 225 over 34, and x is about 2.5725. The two points are opposite each other through the centre, so the chord is twice the distance from the origin to either one, and that distance is x times the square root of 2, giving about 7.28. Checking the point on the curve directly, 2.5725 squared over 25 plus the same over 9 comes back to exactly 1.
questions.hint: The line passes through the centre, so the chord is twice the radius in that direction.

questions.learningObjective: write the chord of a circle from its midpoint alone
questions.practice: writing a chord from its midpoint
questions.stem: The circle with equation x squared plus y squared equals 30 has a chord whose midpoint is the point (2, 5). What is the equation of that chord?

options.misconception: uses the radius squared as the constant instead of the midpoint's own value
swaps the coordinates when forming the coefficient pair
doubles the constant, as though the chord were twice as far out

questions.explanation: The radius to the midpoint of a chord is perpendicular to the chord, so the chord has the form h x + k y equal to a constant, and passing it through (2, 5) fixes that constant as 2 times 2 plus 5 times 5 = 29. Solving that line against the circle gives the discriminant 2900 and two points whose average is exactly (2, 5), and each satisfies x squared + y squared = 30, so the equation is right. Option B uses 30, which is the radius squared, but the constant in a midpoint chord is the squared distance of the midpoint, and here that is 29 and not 30.
questions.hint: The chord is perpendicular to the radius through its midpoint, so build the line from (2, 5) and pass it through (2, 5).

questions.stem: The conic with equation x squared plus 2xy plus y squared equals 25 has a tangent at the point (3, 2). Which line is that tangent?

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: recognise a repeated line as a degenerate conic
questions.stem: A student rewrites the conic x squared plus 2xy plus y squared equals 0 as a sum of squares, concludes that both squares must vanish, and reports a single point at the origin. What is correct?

options.text: the conic degenerates into the line x + y = 0 counted twice, so it holds infinitely many points
the conic is the single point at the origin, since only there do both squares vanish
options.misconception: treats a perfect square as a pair of independent squares

options.text: the conic is empty, since a sum of squares can never equal zero
options.misconception: applies the sum-of-squares rule to a form that is only one square

options.text: the conic is a parabola with vertex at the origin and axis along the line y = x
options.misconception: reads a degenerate equation as a genuine curve of unbounded extent

questions.explanation: The three terms are not independent squares but a single perfect square, since x squared + 2xy + y squared = (x + y) squared, so the equation is (x + y) squared = 0 and its locus is the whole line x + y = 0. Every point of that line satisfies it, for instance (3, -3) and (-7, 7), so the solution set is infinite, which is what makes the conic degenerate. Option C applies the sum-of-squares rule to a form that is really one square repeated, and a single square does vanish at many points.
questions.hint: Look for a perfect square before assuming the terms are independent squares.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: reject a horizontal asymptote that the degrees rule out
questions.stem: A student claims that the rational function with numerator x cubed plus 2x and denominator x squared plus 1 has a horizontal asymptote at y = 1. What is correct?

options.text: there is no horizontal asymptote, because the numerator has the higher degree; the slant asymptote is y = x
the asymptote is y = 1, since both terms are already written over the same denominator
options.misconception: reads a shared denominator as a reason for a shared limit

options.text: the asymptote is y = 0, since every rational function tends to zero at infinity
options.misconception: assumes a limit of zero for all rational functions regardless of degree

options.text: the asymptote is y = x, and it counts as horizontal because it is a straight line
options.misconception: equates being a line with being horizontal

questions.explanation: A horizontal asymptote only exists when the degrees are equal or the numerator's degree is smaller, and here the numerator has degree 3 against the denominator's 2, so the graph climbs without bound and the student is wrong. Long division confirms the line: dividing x cubed + 2x by x squared + 1 gives a quotient of x and a remainder of x, since x times the denominator is x cubed + x. That leftover x over x squared + 1 tends to 0, so the slant asymptote is y = x and it is a line that is not horizontal.
questions.hint: Compare the degrees first; if the numerator wins, the graph approaches a slanted line.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: explain how a chord can be found from its midpoint alone
questions.stem: Explain why the chord of a conic with a given midpoint can be written down without knowing the two endpoints.

answer.exemplar: For a circle the argument is geometric. The line from the centre to the midpoint of a chord is perpendicular to that chord, so with the midpoint at h, k the chord must be the line h x plus k y equal to a constant, and passing the line through the midpoint fixes the constant as h squared plus k squared. No endpoint enters. For a general conic write the quadratic part as a symmetric matrix, and the same substitution that produces the tangent, replacing each x squared by x x0 and each y squared by y y0 while leaving the mixed terms alone, produces the chord whose midpoint is the given point. The reason the two coincide is that a chord midpoint and a tangent point play the same algebraic role: both are the place where a first-order expression can be anchored to the curve. A check is available without any geometry, since substituting the resulting line into the conic gives a quadratic in one variable, and the average of its two roots must come back as the stated midpoint. What does not carry over is the circle's perpendicularity, since a radius to a chord midpoint is not perpendicular to the chord for an ellipse with unequal semi-axes, so the algebraic rule is the part that generalises.

questions.explanation: A model answer must give the circle's perpendicularity argument and then show that the same substitution that yields a tangent yields the midpoint chord, since that transfer is the substance of the rule.
questions.hint: Start from the circle, where the radius is perpendicular to the chord, and then find the algebraic version.

questions.stem: For the hyperbola with equation x squared over 9 minus y squared over 16 equals 1, first find the distance from the centre to a focus, then find the length of the chord through that focus that is perpendicular to the transverse axis, and report the second value.

options.text: about 10.67
about 5.00

options.text: about 5.33
options.misconception: halves the chord by giving only the side above the axis

options.text: about 21.33
options.misconception: doubles the chord a second time after halving it once

questions.explanation: The denominators give a squared = 9 and b squared = 16, and for a hyperbola the focal distance is the square root of 9 + 16 = 5, which is the first stage. Substituting x = 5 into the curve gives 25 over 9 minus y squared over 16 equals 1, so y squared over 16 is 16 over 9 and y equals 16/3, so the chord runs from -16/3 to 16/3 and measures 32/3, about 10.67. That is the general rule 2b squared over a, and it comes to the same figure from the formula, 2 times 16 over 3.
questions.hint: Evaluate the curve at the focal distance to get the half-chord, then double it.

questions.subject: ALGEBRA_II
questions.learningObjective: show that a translation leaves the eccentricity unchanged
questions.stem: The ellipse with equation (x plus 5) squared over 25 plus (y minus 3) squared over 9 equals 1 is a translation of a standard ellipse. First find the distance from its centre to the origin, then find its eccentricity, and report the second value.

options.misconception: reports the first stage instead of the eccentricity
divides the focal distance by the minor axis instead of the major one
inverts the ratio, which would place the value in hyperbola territory

questions.explanation: The brackets give the centre as (-5, 3), and its distance from the origin is the square root of 25 + 9, about 5.83, which is the first stage. The denominators give a = 5 and b = 3, so the focal distance is the square root of 25 - 9 = 4 and the eccentricity is 4 over 5 = 0.8, the second stage. The square-root route agrees, since the eccentricity is the square root of 1 - 9/25, and the point of the item is that the off-centre position changes nothing about the ratio.
questions.hint: Read the centre off the brackets, then use the two semi-axes, which the translation left alone.
